patient.chief_complaint: Acute confusion, agitation, and altered mental status
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. B. is a 61-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C), prior HCC treated with TACE, and a prior HE episode 4 months ago now on rifaximin prophylaxis, brought by his daughter for acute confusion and agitation over the preceding 24 hours. His daughter reported he was found disoriented in the bathroom at 2 AM, had been slurring his speech since yesterday evening, and had been combative and uncooperative throughout the morning. She found an empty vodka bottle in his room, and he admitted on direct questioning to having drunk 'a little yesterday.' His serum ethanol level on arrival was 14 mg/dL — a low but detectable level. He had last been seen by hepatology 3 weeks ago when labs showed stable MELD 18. Over the prior week, his daughter noticed decreasing oral intake, reduced rifaximin adherence (ran out 5 days ago and had not refilled), and increasing abdominal distension. He denied hematemesis or melena. Temperature 37.9°C raised concern for possible infection as a precipitant. The combination of low-level ethanol exposure, rifaximin non-adherence for 5 days, fever, and tachycardia created a moderate-difficulty clinical scenario with multiple potential precipitants requiring careful evaluation. Precipitant was ultimately determined to be combined: alcohol use (direct neurotoxin + ammoniagenic substrate) and rifaximin non-adherence with possible SBP.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD 19) with treated HCC — precipitated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (ascitic PMN 310/mm³) plus rifaximin non-adherence and recent alcohol use.

differential.diagnosis: Septic encephalopathy from SBP (primary precipitant rather than separate diagnosis)
differential.key_features: Ascitic PMN 310/mm³ confirms SBP; cytokine-driven hyperammonemia and reduced hepatic clearance both contribute — treat as HE precipitated by SBP rather than 'septic encephalopathy' alone.
Ethanol 14 mg/dL is too low to drive grade III obtundation in a tolerant alcoholic; withdrawal risk exists 48-72 h post-stop and warrants monitoring with non-benzodiazepine first-line measures.
Coagulopathy (INR 2.2) + thrombocytopenia raise risk; non-contrast CT head excludes hemorrhage.
Chronic alcohol use places patient at risk; no ophthalmoplegia / classic triad; give empiric thiamine before dextrose regardless.
Solitary 1.8 cm post-TACE HCC; no focal deficits; MRI would assess if clinical course atypical.

optimal_actions.action: Comprehensive labs: CMP including AST/ALT/bilirubin/INR/albumin, ammonia, CBC, glucose, electrolytes (Na, K, Mg), BUN/Cr, lactate, blood cultures and urine cultures; toxicology if substance use plausible. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Cirrhosis confirmed (INR 2.2, bilirubin 5.2, albumin 2.1); ammonia 88; WBC 12.4; ethanol low-level; thrombocytopenia 62. Blood cultures sent to screen for sepsis.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No acute intracranial process — hemorrhage and mass effect excluded despite coagulopathy.

optimal_actions.action: Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (AASLD/EASL HE precipitant management; SBP empiric therapy; rifaximin secondary prophylaxis).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering spironolactone, furosemide, propranolol, lactulose, rifaximin — confirm hepatic dosing and screen for any sedatives; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and culture — mandatory in any cirrhotic with ascites + AMS or fever.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ascitic PMN 310/mm³ — SBP confirmed; start empiric ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily + albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — exclude NCSE in obtunded cirrhotic with grade III HE pattern. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Generalized slowing supports metabolic encephalopathy; no NCSE.

optimal_actions.action: Consult hepatology and critical care (grade III HE) — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.
FDG PET has no role in HE workup; metabolic encephalopathy is reversible with precipitant control and does not require nuclear functional imaging.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Empiric IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily for SBP — initiate immediately on PMN ≥250; do not wait for culture.
IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 — reduces hepatorenal syndrome in SBP (AASLD).
Lactulose to 2-4 soft stools/day plus rifaximin 550 mg BID — restart secondary prophylaxis.
Empiric IV thiamine 100 mg before any dextrose; multivitamin replacement in chronic alcoholic.
Withdrawal protocol with symptom-triggered scoring; prefer phenobarbital or careful gabapentin/clonidine adjuncts; avoid scheduled benzodiazepines given HE.
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not hold antibiotics waiting for culture — empiric therapy on suspected SBP is standard.
Avoid scheduled benzodiazepines for withdrawal in a cirrhotic with overt HE; use the lowest possible doses of short-acting agents (e.g., lorazepam) ONLY for severe withdrawal symptoms.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Infection (especially SBP) is the single most common HE precipitant in decompensated cirrhotics with ascites; diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory.
Rifaximin non-adherence is an under-recognized but very common precipitant of overt HE in patients on secondary prophylaxis.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute grade III obtundation to acute alcohol intoxication and adopt 'wait it out' management.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ethanol at 14 mg/dL cannot cause grade III HE in a tolerant alcoholic; ammonia 88 + ascitic PMN 310 = HE precipitated by SBP.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue HCC progression / brain metastasis workup as primary cause of AMS.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Solitary post-TACE HCC and no focal deficits make CNS metastasis very unlikely; treat HE with SBP precipitant first; MRI only if clinical course atypical.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate HE with SBP as hidden precipitant: alcoholic cirrhosis, concurrent low-level ethanol use, rifaximin non-adherence, fever and leukocytosis — paracentesis reveals SBP PMN 310 as primary precipitant; alcohol withdrawal co-management challenge
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools (labs, CT, lit, drug, paracentesis) plus EEG recommended; multiple co-existing precipitants (SBP + rifaximin non-adherence + recent alcohol + thrombocytopenia/coag) require synthesis but the diagnosis is not in doubt.
